From Dye Intermediates to Copper Cathodes: The Second Life of Kiri Industries

In the last week of December 2025, a payment landed that closed one of the longest corporate battles an Indian company has ever fought abroad. Kiri Industries Limited, an Ahmedabad dyestuff maker, received US$689.03 million for its 37.57% stake in DyStar Global Holdings (Singapore) Pte Ltd, roughly ₹5,860 crore.

For scale, the company that received it had revenue of about ₹840 crore in FY26 and a market capitalisation that has spent most of the past year between ₹2,600 crore and ₹3,400 crore. To understand how a mid-cap dye maker ended up with a windfall larger than its own market value, go back to 1998.

Part One: Ahmedabad, 1998
Kiri Dyes and Chemicals Private Limited was incorporated on 14 May 1998 in Ahmedabad by Manishkumar Pravinchandra Kiri, an electronics engineer with a master's in business management. The early years followed a familiar Gujarat playbook: start with reactive dyes for cotton, then go backwards up the chain so you are not at the mercy of intermediate suppliers. Kiri began making vinyl sulphone in April 2006 and H-Acid in March 2007.

That second move mattered more than it sounded. H-Acid is the backbone intermediate of reactive dyes, the molecule from which most reds, blacks and navies are built. It is also filthy to make: production runs on sulphuric acid and oleum and throws off large volumes of acidic effluent. That is why few companies make it, and why the price behaves the way it does. When a large Chinese H-Acid plant shut in early 2016, Kiri told the exchanges that H-Acid had gone from ₹300-360 a kg to ₹900-1,000, and vinyl sulphone from ₹160-180 to ₹240-275. Intermediates are now the larger half of the standalone business, at 57% of Q1 FY27 revenue against 28% for dyes.

Then came the step that explains what Kiri is doing in 2026. Rather than keep buying the acid its intermediates consume, Kiri built it: in September 2009 it began commercial production at Dudhwada in Vadodara district of sulphuric acid, oleum and chlorosulphonic acid: 180,000 MTPA, sulphur-burning, double absorption, with waste heat routed to a 3.3 MW cogeneration unit. A dye company had taught itself sulphur chemistry, and learned that the acid and the heat are both worth money. Hold that thought.
The year before, Kiri had made its first China connection, a reactive dye joint venture, Lonsen Kiri Chemical Industries Limited, with Well Prospering Ltd, an arm of Zhejiang Longsheng Group. That partnership worked. It still does. It is why the next decision looked reasonable.

Part Two: The German prize and the Chinese partner
DyStar was created in 1995 out of the dyes businesses of Bayer and Hoechst, took in BASF's textile dyes in 2000, and by the mid-2000s held roughly a fifth of the global market. Then came the financial crisis, and its German entities went into insolvency in September 2009. Manish Kiri wanted it, could not fund it alone, and went back to Longsheng.

The structure they built in early 2010 is the hinge of this story. A Singapore vehicle, DyStar Global Holdings, acquired the assets through Kiri's subsidiary Kiri Holding Singapore, and Kiri Industries was the majority shareholder. Longsheng put in the bulk of the money, but it came in through Well Prospering as a €22 million zero-coupon convertible bond, convertible into ordinary shares at S$10 apiece, at any time. In February 2010 the assets of DyStar Textilfarben GmbH and 36 subsidiaries changed hands.

A dye maker from Ahmedabad now owned the biggest name in global dyes.

Part Three: The conversion
DyStar bled through FY11 and FY12 as it was restructured. Then, in July 2012, the convertible bond was transferred from Well Prospering to Senda International Capital Limited, another wholly owned Longsheng subsidiary. On 26 December 2012, at the moment DyStar was turning profitable, Senda converted the entire bond into equity at S$10 per share.
Senda held 62.43%, Kiri 37.57%. The Indian promoter of the deal was now the minority partner in the asset he had brought to the table.

The timing was cruel twice over. At home, the rupee's 2013 collapse hit unhedged foreign borrowings and Kiri ended up carrying roughly ₹750 crore of debt through a corporate debt restructuring. It had no cash, a minority stake in a business now throwing off serious profit, and no way to reach any of it. Dividends were not declared. A listing was refused. DyStar's purchases from Kiri, promised on preferred-supplier terms in 2010, fell away after 2012.

Part Four: Ten years in a Singapore courtroom
In 2015, Kiri sued Senda and DyStar for minority oppression: related-party transactions, use of intellectual property, suppressed dividends, unauthorised payments to directors, and the collapse in purchases. The case moved to the Singapore International Commercial Court in 2017.
In 2018 the SICC found multiple acts of oppression and ordered Senda to buy Kiri out at fair value; the appellate court substantially upheld that in 2019. The first valuation judgment, in 2021, put the stake at about US$481.6 million; on review in 2023 the SICC raised it to US$603.8 million.

Winning was not the same as being paid. Senda did not pay, the Sheriff's Office of the Supreme Court of Singapore issued notices for the seizure of securities, and Kiri kept funding a war of attrition against a group many times its size.

So in February 2024 the court changed the instrument. Rather than force Senda to buy, it ordered an en bloc sale of DyStar itself, appointed Deloitte Singapore partners as receivers, and gave Kiri priority payment from the proceeds. In 2025 the Court of Appeal upheld that entitlement and awarded interest at 5.33% a year.
The auction ended where it began: a share purchase agreement with Zhejiang Longsheng in May 2025 and, after a contested restructuring in December that Kiri objected to before the court, a final receipt of US$689.03 million. DyStar, valued in the process at about US$1.8 billion, is now wholly owned by Longsheng. Kiri's FY26 consolidated profit came in at roughly ₹5,567 crore on revenue of about ₹840 crore, which tells you where that profit came from.

Part Five: Copper, acid and fertiliser
The obvious question after a windfall like that is what you do with it. Kiri's answer has nothing to do with dyes and everything to do with acid.

At Jafrabad on the Saurashtra coast, through wholly owned subsidiaries Indo Asia Copper Limited and IndoAsia Agrotech Fertilizers Limited, the group is building an integrated copper and fertiliser complex, with Sanjay Sarkar, who has run Lonsen Kiri, as chief executive of the copper business. The logic is import substitution: India consumes roughly 1.8 million tonnes of refined copper a year against domestic output of about 0.8 million tonnes.

The design is a chain, not a plant:
A 500,000 MTPA copper unit, smelting and refining imported concentrate and scrap into cathodes, wire rods, foil and tubes

Recovery of gold, silver and selenium during refining
Sulphur dioxide from the smelter captured and converted into sulphuric acid

That acid feeding a 350,000 MTPA phosphoric acid plant Which feeds 1,050,000 MTPA of NP and NPK fertiliser, with matching bagging capacity

This is the elegant part, and it is the Dudhwada lesson at thirty times the scale. Every copper smelter must deal with the sulphur in its concentrate, so every smelter makes sulphuric acid whether it wants to or not. For most it is a low-value by-product dumped into whatever market is nearby, and a weak acid market can turn a smelter's economics upside down. Kiri is building the demand alongside the supply, turning a compliance problem into phosphoric acid and then fertiliser. Seventeen years after it started burning sulphur for its own intermediates, that chemistry is why this project is meant to earn 25%.

The disclosed numbers: about ₹8,100 crore for copper, ₹3,600 crore for fertilisers and ₹1,600 crore for renewable power and a marine jetty, roughly ₹13,300 crore in all, at a project IRR near 25% and targeted ROE of 22-30%, with Tata Consulting Engineers as owner's engineer. Of a planned ₹4,000 crore of equity, about ₹1,400 crore had been deployed by the Q1 FY27 call, with debt commitments above 50% received and financial closure still pending. Commissioning is phased: tube plant in Q1 FY28, rod plant in Q2 FY28 on imported cathodes, refinery in Q3 FY29, with most revenue expected in FY29 and FY30.

Kiri has also started walking upstream. In April 2026 its subsidiary Equinaire Holdings took assignment of a US$9.76 million loan from Maharlika Investment Corporation, the Philippines' sovereign wealth fund, to Makilala Mining for the Maalinao-Caigutan-Biyog copper-gold project, with an eye on a concentrate offtake. Celsius Resources, a partner in that project, has moved for emergency arbitration over any offtake signed without its consent. Old habits.

Part Six: What the market thinks
The stock is down roughly a third over the past year. Market capitalisation of about ₹3,300 crore sits below the cash received, and price-to-book has been hovering near 0.4.

The bull case is a fortress balance sheet, scarce H-Acid and vinyl sulphone capacity in a chain where China's environmental costs keep rising, and a funded first phase in a metal India lacks.

The bear case is what the discount is pricing. A dyes company with no metallurgical track record is building a greenfield smelter. Standalone EBITDA was negative in FY24, FY25 and FY26; it turned positive in Q1 FY27 at ₹17.3 crore on revenue of ₹295.3 crore, but the quarter's ₹270 crore profit came almost entirely from ₹284 crore of treasury and interest income. Commissioning dates are, by management's own description, dynamic. No dividend or buyback has been announced; instead the board approved 60,82,600 warrants to the promoter group at ₹475 each on 31 August 2026.

Shareholders who waited a decade for a court to vindicate them are now being asked to wait another four years for a smelter.

Manish Kiri has been right about one very large, very unlikely thing before, and patient enough to be proved right against an opponent with far deeper pockets. The next verdict on him will not come from a judge in Singapore, but from a commissioning schedule on the Gujarat coast.

Legal framework for Internet Shutdown in India

Context: During the "Chalo Sansad" protest organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), Mobile Internet Service were shut down in parts of Central Delhi.

Provisions:

~Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunication Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, Telecommunication services may be suspended.

~Suspension can be ordered only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing.

~Orders must be reasoned, published, geographically and temporarily limited and consider whether less restrictive measures are sufficient.

Under the 2024 Rules, a suspension order cannot remain in force for more than 15 days.

Supreme Court Guidelines:

~In Anuradha Bhasin v Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court linked Internet access with freedoms under Articles 19(1) (a) and 19(1)(g).

~Shutdowns must satisfy necessity and proportionality, be the least restrictive measures, and remain open to judicial review.

Suspension can be challenged in court?
Yes. Under Article 226 before a High Court and Article 32 before the Supreme Court.

India's Position:
India recorded about 24 Internet shutdowns in 2026 till July 22; Jammu & Kashmir has recorded the highest cumulative number since 2012.

Statement : IFF condemns the internet shutdown in parts of Central Delhi. No suspension order has been made public.

New Delhi, 20 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the suspension of mobile internet services imposed today, 20 July 2026, in parts of Central Delhi, including the area around Jantar Mantar. The shutdown coincided with the 'Chalo Sansad' march called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on the opening day of the Monsoon Session of Parliament, where thousands of students and young people had gathered to press their demands. Permission for the march was refused. Prohibitory orders were imposed under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023. Routes to Parliament were sealed, and metro stations including, Patel Chowk, Rajiv Chowk and Janpath were closed. Amid reports of the use of force to disperse protesters, mobile internet was then switched off, reportedly "as a precautionary measure". We urge the immediate restoration of all telecommunication services in the capital and an end to internet shutdowns across India.

The developments of today are of immense consequence to the future of our democracy. The voices gathered at Jantar Mantar, and the residents of the national capital, need to be heard the loudest, not silenced en masse.

No order has been made public

At the time of release of this statement, no copy of any suspension order has been published by the Ministry of Home Affairs, the Department of Telecommunications, the Government of NCT of Delhi or the Delhi Police. Residents of the capital do not know which authority directed the shutdown, on what grounds, over which precise areas, for which services, or for what duration. An unpublished order is an unaccountable order. It cannot be challenged before a court, and the judicial review guaranteed by the Supreme Court becomes illusory. Some reports further indicate the deployment of network jammers in parts of Central Delhi, including near Jantar Mantar. Jamming equipment finds no sanction in the legal framework for the suspension of telecommunication services at all. If jammers were deployed, the government must disclose under what legal authority.

Binding safeguards violated

On 10 January 2020, the Supreme Court in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637 held that the freedom of speech and expression, and the freedom to carry on trade or business through the medium of the internet, are protected under Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. The Court directed that every order suspending telecom services must be published. Reasons must be recorded in writing. The restriction must be proportionate, adopting the least restrictive measure available. It cannot continue indefinitely. It is subject to judicial review, and to scrutiny by a review committee.

Parliament has since replaced the framework of the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885. Under Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023, telecommunication services may be suspended only on the occurrence of a public emergency or in the interest of public safety, on the grounds specified in that provision, and for reasons recorded in writing. The Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, notified on 22 November 2024, give effect to this power. A suspension order may be issued only by the Union Home Secretary or the State Home Secretary. An officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary may act in unavoidable circumstances, subject to confirmation by the competent authority within twenty four hours. Every order must clearly define the geographical area and the specific services suspended, and cannot remain in operation beyond fifteen days. Every order must also be published. A Review Committee must meet within five days of the order and record its findings on whether it complies with Section 20(2).

These safeguards are not being followed

If we account for today's shutdown against this legal architecture. The order is unpublished, in breach of Anuradha Bhasin and the Suspension Rules, 2024 alike. No recorded reasons are available to the public despite little to no reports of violence and consistent calls for the protest to be peaceful by the CJP and other organisers. The precise areas and services covered are undisclosed and so is the duration. Whether the competent authority even issued the order cannot be known. Whether the Review Committee will examine it cannot be verified. While the Suspension Rules prescribe no outer time limit for publication, a gap we have previously flagged, it cannot cut against the spirit of the Anuradha Bhasin judgement. A blanket suspension across densely populated parts of the capital, imposed as a "precaution" against a march to Parliament, is the opposite of a narrowly tailored, least restrictive measure. A shutdown timed to a protest restricts the freedoms of speech and assembly at the very moment they matter most.

The human cost of a shutdown

Access to the internet is a digital right on which the exercise of our fundamental freedoms now depends. When the network goes dark in Central Delhi, a journalist at Jantar Mantar cannot file her report or broadcast live. A street vendor on the surrounding roads cannot accept a UPI payment. A gig worker loses a day's earnings. A parent cannot confirm that a child who joined the march is safe. Cutting off communications prevents people from reaching out for help and manufactures panic in a moment which demands calm. These costs fall hardest on daily wage earners and small traders who can least absorb them. Internet based communications also promote trust between people and their government. 

A pattern, not an aberration

Delhi has seen this before. On 19 December 2019, mobile services were suspended for the first time in the capital's history during the protests against the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, in areas including Seelampur, Jamia Nagar and Mandi House. On 26 January 2021, the Ministry of Home Affairs suspended internet services in Singhu, Ghazipur, Tikri, Mukarba Chowk, Nangloi and their adjoining areas during the farmers' protests. According to the #KeepItOn coalition's report released in March 2026, India recorded 65 internet shutdowns in 2025, the highest of any democracy in the world, and accounts for 920 of the 2,102 shutdowns documented globally since 2016. We have consistently advocated against the harm these disruptions cause, from Jammu and Kashmir to Rajasthan, and from Haryana to Manipur, where a shutdown in 2023 ran for over two hundred days. The orders are rarely published on time, and the findings of review committees never see daylight.

Our demands

We call upon the Government of India and the Government of NCT of Delhi to:

1. Immediately restore all suspended telecommunication and internet services in Central Delhi.
2. Publish forthwith every suspension order passed on or around 20 July 2026, together with the reasons recorded in writing, as mandated by Anuradha Bhasin and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024.
3. Disclose the issuing authority, the grounds, the precise areas and services covered, and the period of operation, and clarify whether network jammers were deployed and under what legal authority.
4. Place the order before the Review Committee within five days as required by the Rules, and make its findings public.
5. Reform Section 20(2)(b) of the Telecommunications Act, 2023 to provide for independent prior authorisation and real consequences for unlawful suspensions.

IFF will file applications under the Right to Information Act, 2005 seeking copies of the suspension orders and the records of the Review Committee, and is examining further legal remedies. 

Delhi and all of India deserve better.

Amid heightened tensions and a heavy police presence in Jaipur, the capital of Rajasthan state in India, the local administration has begun demolishing a 44-year-old historic mosque. The operation was carried out on Sunday (June 7) to remove the historic Noorani Mosque, located in the Malviya Nagar area of Jaipur.

The four-story Noorani Mosque located in Malviya Nagar, Jaipur, India, is being demolished by the authorities as part of a road-widening project. In connection with the operation, internet services across the city were suspended for 24 hours, and extensive security measures were put in place.

The Jaipur Development Authority (JDA) claims that the mosque was constructed illegally on leased land. However, the mosque committee has rejected this allegation, stating that the land was legally purchased from a housing society in 1981 before the structure was built.

A large number of police personnel have been deployed in and around the area, drone surveillance is being conducted, and restrictive orders remain in effect throughout the operation. The mosque committee and several opposition lawmakers have criticized the move, alleging that proper procedures were not followed.

Authorities stated that the temporary internet shutdown was imposed to prevent the spread of rumors and misinformation and to maintain law and order during the demolition process. So far, the operation has remained peaceful, with no reports of violence or unrest.

text:
CJI Surya Kant dictates order:

The communications issued by the Bar Council of India to the Vice-Chancellor and Registrar of NALSAR University of Law, recommending action against the students of the 2026 graduating batch, led to the present controversy.

The said communications were withdrawn by the Bar Council of India within 24 hours.

On August 14, 2026, notice was issued with a direction that no punitive action be taken against the students or faculty of NALSAR University of Law by the Bar Council of India or any State Bar Council.

The Chairman of the Bar Council of India is present and states that all the offending communications have been withdrawn and, as such, the matter does not survive for adjudication.

Sr Adv K. Parameshwar, appearing for the petitioners, submits that notwithstanding the withdrawal of the communications, the legal issue raised in the writ petition requires clarification.

On an independent consideration of the issue, we are of the considered opinion that the Advocates Act, 1961, under which the Bar Council of India has been constituted, does not confer any express or implied power upon it to take disciplinary action against students pursuing legal education.

Such power is vested in the university or educational institution in which the students are enrolled. The Bar Council of India may prescribe and enforce standards of legal education in accordance with the statutory provisions and applicable regulations. It cannot, however, take disciplinary action against a law student.

It is sufficient to clarify accordingly.

Having regard to what we have declared above, the communication dated August 13, 2026, and all subsequent modified communications are declared to have been issued without jurisdiction.

The interim direction issued by this Court on August 14, 2026, is made absolute.

The writ petition is disposed of accordingly.

text:
Delay by Customs in re-assessing Bills of Entry and generating correct IGST challans: Bombay High Court directs Department to complete time-bound re-assessment within eight weeks with interim protection from coercive action.

Issue:
Whether the Department could be directed under writ jurisdiction to carry out re-assessment of six Bills of Entry, issue correct Integrated Goods and Services Tax (IGST) payable challans, and grant an upfront waiver of statutory interest.

Rule:
Under the provisions of the Customs Act, 1962 read with Section 3(7) of the Customs Tariff Act, 1975 and the Integrated Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, re-assessment of imported goods and determination of applicable duty/tax liability must be conducted by the proper officer in accordance with binding judicial precedents laid down by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and High Courts. Ancillary statutory levies such as interest fall within the realm of administrative adjudication during the re-assessment proceeding itself.

Application:
The Assessee approached the High Court invoking writ jurisdiction against the Department’s inaction in re-assessing six subject Bills of Entry, generating accurate IGST challans, and seeking relief against levy of interest. The Department fairly conceded to conducting the re-assessment exercise in a time-bound manner, while requesting that the claim for waiver of interest be left open for the proper officer's statutory determination. Adopting this consensus, the Court held that the re-assessment must be finalized in terms of established legal principles without the High Court delving prematurely into the merits or interest waiver.

Conclusion:
The High Court directed the Department to complete the re-assessment of the six Bills of Entry within eight weeks from the date of receipt of the certified copy of the order. While leaving the issue of interest waiver open for the proper officer to decide, the Court granted interim protection to the Assessee, directing that no coercive recovery action be initiated until the re-assessment exercise is completed.

Impact Analysis:
This ruling prevents arbitrary departmental inaction on customs re-assessments and protects importers from coercive recovery during pending adjudication, while reaffirming that statutory claims like interest waiver must first be examined by the adjudicating officer.

🚨 BREAKING: Government of India directs YouTube to take down Dhruv Rathee's (@dhruv_rathee) video titled "Can Hindus Eat Beef? | Kerala Story 2 Exposed."

The Grievance Appellate Committee (GAC), Ministry of Electronics & IT, by its Order dated 15 July 2026 (Appeal No. 8321/2026), has directed YouTube to remove the video within 24 hours of receiving the order.

Note: Although the order is dated 15.07.2026, it was uploaded publicly today (19 July 2026).

Key findings of the GAC:
• The video contains statements found to insult Bhagwan Shri Ram, Bhagwan Shri Krishna, and Sita Devi.
• It was found to make claims that they consumed meat and alcohol using disputed interpretations of scriptures.
• The GAC held that the content hurts the religious sentiments of crores of Hindus and is contrary to societal harmony.
• YouTube's free speech arguments were not accepted, with the order noting that freedom of expression is subject to the reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

The order follows the Hon'ble Delhi High Court's direction dated 3 July 2026 requiring the appeal to be decided within 15 days.

The complainant has also stated that these findings may be relevant to a separate pending petition before a Magistrate seeking registration of an FIR against Dhruv Rathee, which is listed for hearing on 10 September 2026.

"Faith cannot be mocked under the garb of content creation. Justice is being delivered step by step."

Jai Shri Ram 🙏

Special thanks to Sr. Adv. Makarand D. Adkar Ji (@AdkarMakarand) for his guidance and support, and to the legal team for their efforts.

Department attempts to penalise an Independent Director under GST Section 122(1A); Bombay High Court steps in to grant interim protection against coercive recovery.

Issue:
Whether an individual serving as an Independent Director of a company comes within the scope of penalty provisions under Section 122(1A) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, and whether interim protection against coercive recovery is warranted.

Rule:
Section 122(1A) of the CGST Act, 2017 prescribes penal liability only on any person who retains the benefit of specified fraudulent transactions or at whose instance such transactions are conducted; as judicially interpreted by the Coordinate Bench in Shantanu Sanjay Hundekari, an individual acting in a non-beneficiary or official capacity does not automatically fall under the sweep of this section.

Application:
The Assessee was subjected to penalty proceedings under Section 122(1A) in an individual capacity while serving merely as an Independent Director of the company. The Assessee contended that he was not the company itself nor did he fall within the ambit of the penal provision, relying upon the Coordinate Bench ruling which had attained finality as the Supreme Court did not interfere with it. Upon examining the statutory provision and binding precedent, the High Court observed that a strong prima facie case was established in favour of the Assessee.

Conclusion:
Since a strong prima facie case was made out by the Assessee based on established judicial precedent, the High Court granted ad-interim relief and directed the Department not to take any coercive action regarding the penalty in question until further orders.

Impact Analysis:
This order reaffirms that the Department cannot routinely invoke Section 122(1A) against independent directors or corporate professionals in their individual capacities, offering vital interim immunity from coercive tax recovery where no direct personal involvement or retention of illicit benefit is established.

Statement : The blocking of BitChat's code on GitHub is unconstitutional and authoritarian. 

New Delhi, 24 July 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) condemns the order issued by the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), Ministry of Home Affairs, directing GitHub to remove the code repositories of BitChat. 

The order, Notice No. 11072601011432, was issued at 11:16 pm on 23 July 2026 under Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act, 2000 read with Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021. The order directs GitHub to disable access to three repositories, including the Android application and its release files, within three hours. It threatens the platform with loss of safe harbour and criminal prosecution. No copy was published by the Government of India. The public learnt of it from a post by @jack, whose team develops BitChat. Censorship in India now comes to light through disclosure by the censored.

Since 17 July 2026, the Ministry of Home Affairs has suspended mobile internet around Jantar Mantar as per public reports about five times, most recently within a 1.5 kilometre radius from 4 pm until midnight on 23 July. That radius takes in Janpath and parts of Connaught Place. Reports describe signal jammers at the protest site and people walking two kilometres before their phones work. Inside that zone a student separated from her group during a detention drive cannot send a message to say where she is. Thousands of students and young people have camped at Jantar Mantar since June, seeking accountability for examination irregularities. Permission for their march to Parliament was refused. Metro stations were shut and also internet connectivity has been blocked.

BitChat is an open source application built for exactly this situation. It passes messages from phone to phone over Bluetooth, without mobile networks or a central server. It is striking that the order does not identify a single unlawful message. It objects to what BitChat is. In its own words, the application is dangerous because it enables communication "even during network restrictions" and can "circumvent lawful restrictions" during "internet shutdowns". Hence, the government's objection is that citizens can speak to one another while it has switched the internet off. 

The order is illegal on at least four grounds. 

1. Section 79(3)(b) is not a blocking power. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down the provision. Intermediaries may be required to act only on a court order, or a government notification confined to the grounds under Article 19(2) of the Constitution. Blocking is governed exclusively by Section 69A and the Blocking Rules, 2009, which require a hearing and reasons recorded in writing, subject to review. Directions issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal evade these safeguards, and constitutional challenges to this parallel regime are pending before High Courts. 

2. The reasons in the order are circular. The order asserts that the repositories contain "information which is prohibited under any law" without naming any such information, and rests on what the application is "capable of" enabling. Anticipated misuse of a communications tool is not a lawful basis to prohibit the tool. By this logic a telephone exchange could be sealed. 

3. The order cites Section 43 of the IT Act, a civil compensation provision, alongside conspiracy and abetment offences under the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, against a platform that hosts code. 

4. A three hour deadline issued close to midnight forecloses legal assessment and recourse, and fails the proportionality standard in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637.

The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code.

IFF demands that the Government of India:

1. Withdraw Notice No. 11072601011432 dated 23 July 2026 issued to GitHub.
2. Publish every takedown direction issued under Section 79(3)(b), Rule 3(1)(d) and the Sahyog Portal, with the reasons recorded for each.
3. Restore full connectivity around Jantar Mantar, publish all suspension orders, and disclose the legal authority for the deployment of jammers.

We stand with the developers and the young protesters whose speech this order seeks to silence.

Sound the Alarm : IFF’s First Read on MeitY's Draft IT Rules Second Amendment, 2026

New Delhi, 30 March 2026

On 30 March 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology published proposed amendments to the IT Rules, 2021, inviting public comments by 14 April,  a comment period of barely fifteen days for changes with far reaching consequences for free speech and intermediary governance in India. We have conducted a quick review of the draft amendments. Despite being presented as "clarificatory and procedural," they represent a dangerous expansion of executive power over online speech.

We wish to state at the outset that these proposed amendments need to be immediately withdrawn and every member in our citizenry should demand their roll back and stand with the Constitution of India. These proposed amendments come at a time of fear and increased government directed censorship, especially of online political speech that includes parody and satire of the government, including the Prime Minister.

In brief the five changes are listed below:

1. Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h): Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law.

2. Rule 3(4): Insertion of a new clause that mandates intermediary compliance with MeitY-issued clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines, making such compliance a condition for retaining safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act. These are not anchored to the rule making powers of the IT Act, 2000 and provide uncanalised power to MEITY despite it stating otherwise.

3. Rule 8(1) proviso: A substitution in the proviso that expands applicability of MIB’s oversight mechanism in Part III of the rules to:  (1) intermediaries and (2) users who are not “publishers” and post/share news and current affairs content online. This oversight mechanism contains the blocking powers of MIB by way of Rule 14 (Inter-Departmental Committee), Rule 15 (Procedure for issuing directions to block), and Rule 16 (Emergency blocking provisions).

4. Rule 14(2) : A substitution that expands the scope of the IDC from hearing "complaints or grievances" to hearing "matters", including those referred by the Ministry of Information and Broadcasting.

5. Rule 14(5) : Replaces "complaints or grievances" with "the matter" in relation to IDC examination and recommendations.

A massive expansion of an unconstitutional censorship and regulatory power

First and most concerningly, Rule 3(4) creates a sweeping power for MeitY to issue binding instruments which are not anchored in law such as clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs, codes of practice, and guidelines that intermediaries must comply with as a condition of safe harbour under Section 79 of the IT Act.

The Supreme Court's 2015 judgment in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) 5 SCC 1, remains the foundational precedent governing intermediary liability. It constrains the proposed amendments in several ways. First, the court read down Section 79(3)(b) to require that "actual knowledge" of unlawful content must come through a court order or government notification. Any Rule 3(4) making MeitY, "clarifications, advisories, directions, SOPs", lower the constitutional threshold for intermediary due diligence obligations.

Further, the settled principle in Indian administrative law, reaffirmed in Indian Express Newspapers v. Union of India (1985) 1 SCC 641 and Confederation of Ex-Servicemen Associations v. Union of India (2006) 8 SCC 399, is that delegated legislation must remain within the four corners of the parent statute.  It is important to note that the rule-making power under Section 87(1) of the IT Act is confined to, "carry[ing] out the provisions" of the Act. Section 87(2)(zg) authorizes rules for intermediary guidelines under Section 79(2), and Section 87(2)(z) for blocking procedures under Section 69A(2). Justice Chandurkar's judgement in the Kunal Kamra case clearly found the FCU amendment was not properly referable to either provision. Hence, any Rule 3(4) mandating compliance with MeitY advisories would face identical challenges since they create substantive new obligations not contemplated by Sections 79 or 87.

Even though Rule 3(4)(b)(ii) states that such, “advisories” etc. need to, “clearly specify the statutory provision or legal basis under which it is issued”, since these are not required to be published or made public there is every likelihood these will be issued with secrecy and hence may just in a tautological manner refer back to Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. This is similar to a logical fallacy in which it is clearly observable that a student is cheating on an exam who then claims that they may be permitted to continue cheating since they are stating at the same time they are not cheating. 

The practical effect of Rule 3(4) is that intermediaries face a perpetual compliance threat. Any failure to comply with any MeitY-issued instrument, however vague, however rapidly issued may cost them their safe harbour. The response for an intermediary is over-compliance and over-censorship.

Circumventing existing stay orders

The original proviso to Rule 8(1) stated that Part III applied to intermediaries only "for the purposes of rules 15 and 16"  i.e., content blocking directions and emergency blocking. The amended proviso now extends this to Rule 14, bringing intermediaries and user-generated news/current affairs content under the jurisdiction of the Inter-Departmental Committee.

Under Rules 9(1) and 9(3) of the 2021 IT Rules, there is a Code of Ethics compliance requirement and the three-tier grievance redressal mechanism, both of which were stayed by the Bombay High Court on 14 August 2021 as prima facie violative of Article 19(1)(a) and ultra vires the IT Act. On the oversight mechanism in Rules 14, 15, and 16, the Bombay High Court granted the petitioners to seek relief on this rule when an Inter Departmental Committee is established. The Madras High Court affirmed this stay as having pan-India effect in its order of 16 September 2021 in T.M. Krishna v. Union of India, observing that "an oversight mechanism to control the media by the government may rob the media of its independence." 

Both these cases, along with other cases challenging various provisions of the 2021 IT Rules, are now pending adjudication before the Delhi High Court.

The expansion of Rule 8(1) to cover Rules 14, 15, and 16 is an attempt to expand the blocking powers of MIB to both intermediaries and users who are not “publishers” but post news and current affairs content online. The IDC can now examine "matters" relating to user-generated news content on intermediary platforms without the Code of Ethics framework having been adjudicated as constitutional; the government effectively obtains the content oversight machinery that three High Courts found illegal, through a different procedural door.

Transforming the IDC from Grievance Body to Censorship Apparatus

The original Rule 14(2) required the IDC to hear "complaints regarding violation or contravention of the Code of Ethics." The amended version removes this requirement entirely. 

The IDC now hears:
(a) grievances arising from decisions at Level I or II; or
(b) "matters" referred to by the Ministry.

Clause (b) is unconstrained since, (a) there is no requirement that the "matter" arise from a complaint, (b) no requirement that the "matter" relate to a Code of Ethics violation; and (c) no requirement that the affected party be heard before the referral. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting can, on its own motion, refer any content-related "matter" to the IDC. 

The cumulative effect of the amendments to Rules 8 and 14 is to reconstruct the oversight machinery that the Bombay and Madras High Courts found constitutionally suspect, in a form designed to evade the existing interim orders. The IDC, previously limited to the three-tier complaints process under the stayed Rules 9(3), 12, and 13 framework, now operates as a free-standing censorship committee that can take up "matters" referred by the executive.

Increased user surveillance through mandatory data retention directions

Insertion of phrases within existing clauses making data retention obligations under the IT Rules additional to retention requirements under any other law. For instance, the mandatory data retention of user data beyond 180 days within Rule 3(1)(g) and 3(1)(h) may be prescribed for longer periods and other purposes raising risks of surveillance and even potentially data leaks of sensitive data that is stored for longer periods of time. Government mandates for data retention as to their legal authority and hence period of retention will be beyond those contained under the IT Act.

SOS for Digital Rights 

IFF urges an urgent rollback!

We are alarmed by the continuing expansion of unchecked executive power that is opposed to the Constitution of India. The present actions of MEITY smack of digital authoritarianism and we call on them to withdraw these proposed amendments. 

The proper course is to await judicial determination of the pending challenges, respect interim protections granted by constitutional courts, and pursue regulatory objectives through parliamentary legislation rather than subordinate instruments that exceed the parent statute.

If not withdrawn, IFF will file a detailed response before the comment deadline. We call upon all stakeholders to submit their objections before 14 April 2026 at itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

The smallest corporate penalty under DPDP is ₹50 crore. That is the residual entry in the Schedule, covering breach of any provision of the Act or the Rules that is not separately listed.

Set that against what compliance costs. For a mid-sized Indian company a DPDP programme runs to a few crore and takes three to four quarters end to end. Most of that time is discovery rather than remediation, because you cannot fix data flows you have not mapped and very few companies hold a current map.

The arithmetic is not close, and the pressure sits in the calendar rather than the cost.

Full enforcement begins 13 May 2027. If a programme takes three to four quarters and you want it finished rather than in progress on that date, the comfortable start date has already passed.

That does not mean a company starting now cannot get there. It means the sequence matters more than it did. Data inventory first, then a gap assessment, then remediation ordered by penalty exposure rather than by what is easiest to fix.

Editorial: “Unkind cuts” — ECI’s voter deletions

Core Idea

Editorial questions the large-scale deletion of voters during the Election Commission of India’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in Telangana and Karnataka.

1. Scale of deletions

Around 22% voters in Telangana and 19.5% in Karnataka were reportedly deleted.

Bengaluru saw some constituencies losing more than half their electors.

Hyderabad had several constituencies with over 40% deletions.

Such massive deletions cannot simply be dismissed as routine cleaning of electoral rolls.

2. Why is it problematic?

If voters have merely migrated within the same State, their names should be shifted rather than deleted.

The editorial argues that available survey and population data do not sufficiently justify such large reductions.

Therefore, transparency + verification become essential.

3. Democratic concern

The right to vote is central to universal adult franchise.
Wrongful deletion can lead to disenfranchisement—a citizen being effectively excluded from democratic participation.

4. Institutional accountability

ECI has reportedly not provided adequate elector-to-population ratios and detailed deletion data.

Karnataka’s deletion lists lacked easily verifiable details such as old booth numbers, making verification difficult.

Political parties and citizens also need to actively file objections.

5. Larger lesson

Electoral-roll revision is necessary to remove dead, duplicate or shifted voters, but the process must never sacrifice legitimate voters.

Way Forward:
Transparency → searchable deletion lists → door-to-door verification → easy claims & objections → independent audit → timely restoration of wrongly deleted names.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

The Press Club of India expresses grave concern over the recent spate of takedown orders issued across social media platforms targeting content critical of the government, where creators have been blocked or their material removed.

The PCI Managing Committee strongly opposes these instances of blatant executive overreach and demands that the authorities respect citizens' and journalists' fundamental right to freedom of speech and expression enshrined in and protected by Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution.

FREE SPEECH DOESN’T NEED A GOVERNMENT PERMISSION SLIP.

The Modi Government’s growing agenda for controlling what Indians can see, read, post, critique and challenge online should concern every citizen — regardless of political affiliation.

From demanding takedowns to tightening the time available to platforms to scrutinise government notices, the direction is unmistakable: comply first, question later. India’s 2026 IT-rule changes cut the takedown window for unlawful content to just three hours, while the Government has also proposed making certain official advisories legally binding on platforms. (Reuters⁠)

That is precisely why Elon Musk’s decision to resist, scrutinise and challenge government demands rather than blindly obey every request matters.

X’s own stated policy is that requests can be challenged when they are legally defective, overly broad or appear to impermissibly burden freedom of expression. (Transparency⁠)

And that is where the real problem begins for the Modi Government.

When an independent platform refuses to become an obedient extension of the State, the State’s attempts to control the narrative become visible.

No algorithm can hide that.
No press conference can spin that.
No amount of propaganda can erase that.

If the Government’s demands are genuinely about protecting citizens and enforcing legitimate law, let them withstand public scrutiny, judicial scrutiny and independent platform scrutiny.

But if criticism, dissent, inconvenient facts and uncomfortable questions are increasingly treated as “content to be removed”, then Musk’s resistance does something far more important than defending X.

It exposes this Govt’s vile intent and its surreptitious machinery.

And once the machinery is exposed, the Modi Government stands increasingly bare before the very citizens whose freedom of expression it claims to protect.

A democracy doesn’t become stronger by silencing criticism.
It becomes stronger by surviving it. 

There seems to be a crackdown on Modi Govt these days from every corner and every cross section of India. Are “Acche Din” finally around the corner for India ⁉️

quotedTweet.text:
Statement: Delhi Police's facial recognition sweep at Jantar Mantar is unreliable and unlawful: the list of 2,873 must be withdrawn

New Delhi, 4 September 2026

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is gravely concerned by The Indian Express's investigation, published today, into the Delhi Police's claim that its Facial Recognition System (FRS) identified 2,873 persons with "criminal antecedents" at the Jantar Mantar protests of 20 to 26 July 2026. Of the 205 persons accused of murder, rape and attempt to murder whom it checked, the Express found that at least 25 were lodged in Tihar, Mandoli or Rohini jails when the software placed them at the protest. Some had been in custody for years. This is not a marginal error as it displays a 12 per cent rate of demonstrable impossibility in the only sample independently verified, with no reason to believe the remaining 2,668 names are any better. Yet on 1 September 2026, at the Union's request, the Supreme Court, while quashing all FIRs against student protesters under Article 142, permitted the Delhi Police to register "fresh and specific" FIRs against these 2,873 persons. The Court was entitled to assume that the sworn affidavit of 17 August 2026 rested on verified facts, however these appear to be subject to further verification. 

A system the police know to be unreliable

In a 2022 RTI reply to IFF, the Delhi Police disclosed that it treats a match as "positive" at a similarity score of just 80 per cent, and retains lower-scoring "false positives" for "empirical investigation". The system was procured in 2018 under the Delhi High Court's orders in Sadhan Haldar v. NCT of Delhi to trace missing children; the Court was later told its accuracy was around 2 per cent. A tool bought to find lost children is now building dossiers on protesters, which is a function creep. 

In K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) 10 SCC 1, nine judges held that any intrusion into privacy must satisfy legality, necessity and proportionality. Legality requires a law, and there is none. The Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 permits "measurements", including photographs, to be taken only from persons convicted, arrested or detained (Sections 3 to 5), not the scanning of every face at a lawful assembly against a police database. Neither the Delhi Police Act, 1978 nor the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 confers such a power. The "Crime Kundli" database against which 2,402 of these matches were run has no disclosed statutory basis or retention limit, and the affidavit does not say whether the 2,873 are convicts, accused, or merely named in a case.

A disproportionate assault on the right to protest

In Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018) 17 SCC 324, the Supreme Court held that peaceful protest at Jantar Mantar is protected by Articles 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(b), and Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) 3 SCC 637 requires the State to choose the least restrictive measure. Sifting thousands of faces to single out people for their status rather than their conduct fails every limb of that test. It also inverts the presumption of innocence: "field verification" means police at the doors of 2,873 households whose only established act is, at most, attending a protest, or, as the Express shows, not even that. The Court of Appeal of England and Wales held live facial recognition unlawful in R (Bridges) v. Chief Constable of South Wales Police [2020] EWCA Civ 1058 for leaving "too much discretion" to individual officers. Further, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (A/HRC/48/31, 2021) has called for a moratorium on remote biometric identification in public spaces, and the EU's AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, Article 5(1)(h)) prohibits it for law enforcement save in narrow, judicially authorised cases.

Our demands

In July 2026, IFF wrote to the Commissioner of Police, Delhi, seeking an end to live facial recognition at protest sites, deletion of protesters' facial templates and match results, and publication of the governing SOPs. Those demands stand. Today we further call upon:

1. The Delhi Police to withdraw the list of 2,873 persons, place the Express's findings before the Supreme Court, and suspend all "field verification" pending an independent technical audit of the FRS;

2. The Union Government to impose a moratorium on facial recognition at public assemblies;

3. Parliament to enact a statutory framework for biometric surveillance with prior judicial authorisation, retention limits and independent oversight;

4. The Supreme Court to be informed that the affidavit it relied upon has been shown to be wrong and subject to further verification.

IFF has assisted content creator @shristhikhanna  in challenging the nationwide withholding of her Instagram account, @ shrishtii.khanna. On 7 July 2026, her account, which had over 1,03,000 followers, was blocked in India under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act. She received no prior notice, no hearing, and no information about which government agency had ordered the block. After approaching the Delhi High Court, she was finally able to obtain a copy of the blocking order. (1/7)
Read More: https://t.co/2DU2p5eYcA

The case raises a larger question about the use of Section 79(3)(b) and the Sahyog framework. The provision refers to removing or disabling access to specific “material” or “information”. Yet here, an entire account containing years of existing work, along with all future speech, was blocked nationwide. This amounts to a far more sweeping restriction than the removal of an individual post. (6/7)

In Shreya Singhal Case (2015), the Supreme Court upheld intermediary obligations under Section 79(3)(b) on the understanding that they would operate pursuant to court orders or government notifications consistent with Article 19(2). An automated, unsigned order that identifies no specific post, provides no hearing, and blocks an entire account raises serious questions about proportionality, natural justice and procedural safeguards. With the blocking order now disclosed, Shrishti can challenge the action on its merits before the High Court of Jammu & Kashmir and Ladakh. IFF will continue to support her in this matter. (7/7)

Maharashtra is reportedly considering a new criminal provision specifically targeting “defamatory social media posts”. The proposal, reportedly recommended by a committee headed by Maharashtra’s DGP, raises serious constitutional concerns and risks reviving the spirit of Section 66A of the IT Act, which the Supreme Court struck down in Shreya Singhal in 2015. IFF has written to the DGP urging reconsideration. (1/7)

Read More: https://t.co/LVeOWBg2xC

The timing of such proposals also matters. India is already witnessing an extraordinary expansion of online content restrictions, with nearly 1.95 lakh blocking orders reportedly issued to major platforms between March and July 2026. At a time when social media remains one of the few accessible spaces for citizens to criticise governments and participate in public debate, new criminal restrictions demand particular scrutiny. (6/7)

IFF has sent a representation to Maharashtra’s DGP urging the Committee not to recommend a separate “social media defamation” offence, and has sought transparency around its proposed amendments through an RTI. When the order was finally obtained through litigation, it referred to an entirely unrelated individual. IFF has now sought a review and restoration of the reel.

The blocking order itself raised serious concerns. It referred to a person named Mr. Vemireddy Prabhakar Reddy, who is entirely unknown to the journalists and has no connection whatsoever with the reel, which featured interviews with residents of Tarluvada village. The journalists were also never given an opportunity to respond or defend their reporting. (6/7)

IFF has now issued a legal notice seeking a periodic review of the blocking under the IT Rules, 2021, a proper hearing for the journalists, disclosure of the grounds for the restriction, and restoration of the reel. A factual ground report affecting freedom of speech and journalistic work cannot be restricted through an opaque process without procedural safeguards. (7/7)
